analysis.one_liner: Repeals a dozen tax breaks for oil and gas companies, including drilling deductions and percentage depletion.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee in March 2021 but never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end a set of special tax rules that lower the tax bills of oil and gas companies. It repeals deductions and credits for drilling and production, including percentage depletion, intangible drilling costs, credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, and a 24-month write-off for exploration costs. It also bans a favorable inventory accounting method (LIFO) for the biggest integrated oil companies, limits a foreign tax credit for companies paying levies to foreign governments, and extends the federal petroleum excise tax to oil from tar sands and oil shale. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly, because closing these tax breaks would raise federal revenue and put oil companies on the same footing as other businesses. Communities affected by drilling and oil pollution benefit indirectly, since the tax rules being repealed exist to reward more drilling, and the excise tax change would extend spill-tax funding to tar sands and oil shale oil.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and communities near drilling

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals percentage depletion and the deduction for intangible drilling and development costs, two of the largest long-standing oil and gas tax breaks, and repeals credits for producing from marginal wells and for enhanced oil recovery.
It extends the write-off period for geological and geophysical (exploration) expenditures from 24 months to seven years, meaning companies pay tax on exploration spending sooner.

It bars major integrated oil companies — those producing at least 500,000 barrels of crude a day with over $1 billion in receipts — from using last-in, first-out (LIFO) inventory accounting, which lowers reported income and defers tax.

It limits the foreign tax credit for dual capacity taxpayers, companies that pay a levy to a foreign country and receive specific economic benefits in return, and expands the definition of crude oil for excise tax purposes to include oil from tar sands and oil shale.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies bear the cost, from the largest integrated majors (LIFO and foreign tax credit changes) to small independent producers (percentage depletion, marginal-well credit, drilling cost deductions). Some of the higher cost of production could be passed to consumers through fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers of all sizes

drawbacks.text: Repealing drilling-related deductions and credits raises the after-tax cost of producing oil and gas, and companies can pass part of that cost to consumers in the form of higher fuel prices.

The repeal of the marginal-well credit and percentage depletion falls hardest on small independent producers and stripper-well operators rather than the majors, which could accelerate well shutdowns and cost jobs in oil-producing regions.
The bill only raises revenue by closing breaks; it does not directly lower anyone's energy bills or direct the money to any specific public purpose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward tax-fairness measure: it removes preferences that let oil and gas companies pay less than other businesses, and its main costs fall on the industry, with some risk of modestly higher fuel prices passed to consumers. Its weakness is that it is purely subtractive — it raises revenue without directing it to anything specific and does nothing to reduce energy costs for households. On balance, the benefits (fairer taxation, less subsidy for drilling) outweigh the costs, but the largest cost is borne in oil-dependent communities.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 2021, and the committee never acted on it — no markup, no vote — so it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer (D-OR) introduced the bill on March 26, 2021, with Reps. Casten, McEachin, and Porter as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action after the referral; the action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote.
The bill had 45 cosponsors, all Democrats, by the end of the Congress.
Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off because the bill died: they keep the deductions, credits, and accounting methods the bill would have repealed, at no cost to their tax bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies that kept the tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 26, 2021 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 45 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them controlled committee action on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on March 26, 2021 and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never brought the bill to a committee markup or vote during the 117th Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Beneficiary of the tax breaks at stake
against.what_they_did: The industry has long campaigned to preserve federal oil and gas tax preferences; no evidence of its activity appears in the bill's record, but its stake in the outcome was direct.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Democratic chair of the referral committee never moved the bill, so it advanced nowhere and drew no Republican support.

industries.note: The bill bans LIFO inventory accounting for majors producing 500,000+ barrels a day and limits their foreign tax credit, raising their tax bills. These companies benefit from favorable tax treatment that ordinary taxpayers do not get.

industries.industry: Independent and small oil and gas producers
industries.note: Repealing percentage depletion, the marginal-well credit, and intangible drilling cost deductions removes the breaks that most favor smaller producers. Their interest in keeping the subsidies runs against taxpayers who fund them.

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale producers
industries.note: The bill extends the petroleum excise tax (which funds oil-spill liability programs) to bitumen-derived and oil shale oil, ending their exemption from that tax.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and drilling services
industries.note: Stretching the write-off for geological and geophysical exploration costs from 24 months to seven years makes exploration spending more expensive to finance, reducing the tax incentive that supports demand for drilling work.
